title: Accelerating Catalyst Materials Discovery With Large Artificial Intelligence Models
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into catalysis is fundamentally reshaping the research paradigm of catalyst discovery. Unlike traditional trial-and-error approaches, AI-empowered data-driven technologies, particularly large AI models such as universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs), offer unprecedented capabilities in exploring complex spaces, predicting catalytic performance, and accelerating rational design. Standing at the forefront of data-driven science, we underscore how databases, universal MLIPs, and LLMs are revolutionizing the traditional catalysis paradigm and bridging the ontology-concept-computation-experiment continuum. We then demonstrate significant recent progress, and discuss their potential and challenges in the catalytic field. By leveraging cutting-edge universal MLIPs and LLMs, researchers can conduct large-scale simulations, highly efficient data acquisition, training, and prediction, and even self-directed research in the field of catalysis. Looking ahead, these advantages enable the rapid development of target catalysts, which will be propelled by integrated universal MLIPs, multimodal LLMs, and automation systems. Developments in these domains will pave the way toward AI-empowered closed-loop platforms and cross-disciplinary Digital Materials Ecosystems that broaden the discovery landscape and foster cross-materials innovation, marking the dawn of a new era in which catalyst materials discovery is perpetually accelerating.

title: From Atoms to Reactors: A Critical Review of a Decade of Machine Learning in Heterogeneous Catalysis (2017–2026)
abstract: ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

title: Machine learning approaches for electrocatalyst design in water splitting: a review for green hydrogen production
abstract: The production of green hydrogen through water splitting requires highly efficient electrocatalysts, but the current trial-and-error-based synthesis or discovery is time-consuming, costly and resource-intensive. Machine learning (ML) provides a powerful, data-driven alternative that can model complex structure-activity relationships across large chemical spaces at orders-of-magnitude speed. This review systematically overviews the life cycle of the electrocatalyst research and development application of ML. First, the thermodynamic and kinetic principles of the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions are summarised, along with some well-adopted and accepted activity descriptors. Then we explore data sources, featurization approaches, and algorithms, and discuss the model space, from a simple interpretable model to a graph neural network to a generative model, in the context of the ML toolkit. Strategic applications are discussed for high-throughput virtual screening of alloys and single-atom catalysts, as well as multifunctional activity prediction for overall water splitting, and stability optimisation under operating conditions. The topic of emerging frontiers is highlighted, including high-entropy alloys, amorphous materials, and linking atomic-scale understanding to device-level performance through integration with density functional theory. Finally, the problems of data scarcity, model interpretability and the discrepancy between computational predictions and industrial implementation are discussed, along with future directions for closed-loop discovery and self-driving laboratories. Incorporating ML into electrocatalyst design and combining it with autonomous experimentation will revolutionise this process, from simulation to energy solution, dramatically speeding it up.

title: Boosting Computational Catalysis and Chemical Reactivity with Artificial Intelligence
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are rapidly reshaping the landscape of computational chemistry, offering new opportunities for accelerating catalyst discovery and deepening our understanding of chemical reactivity. This perspective highlights emerging methodologies ranging from machine learning potentials and reinforcement learning to generative AI and large language models that are poised to transform computational catalysis. We discuss challenges in developing robust molecular representations for transition-metal complexes, bridging mechanistic understanding with AI-driven predictions, and constructing reliable data sets that capture both successful and failed reactivity outcomes. By drawing on the authors' practical experience across computational, experimental, and AI-driven domains, we emphasize the importance of integrating chemical intuition and methodological expertise with data-driven approaches while remaining open to serendipitous discoveries enabled by automation and self-driving laboratories. Ultimately, the future of computational catalysis lies in balancing human intuition with algorithmic power, leveraging AI not as a replacement but as an accelerator of chemical insight, mechanistic understanding, and catalyst design.

title: Machine learning-accelerated inverse design of energy materials: A critical review of graph neural networks, physics-informed models, and generative AI for batteries, perovskite solar cells, and electrocatalysts
abstract: The global urgency to transition away from fossil fuels has placed extraordinary pressure on materials scientists to deliver breakthroughs in energy storage, solar energy conversion, and electrocatalysis — and to deliver them faster than the conventional trial-and-error research cycle allows. This review examines, critically and in depth, how machine learning is reshaping that cycle for three pivotal material families: lithium-ion and solid-state battery electrodes and electrolytes, halide perovskite solar absorbers, and transition-metal electrocatalysts for the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions. We pay particular attention to three classes of algorithm that have proven most consequential: graph neural networks (GNNs), which learn directly from the topology and chemistry of crystal structures; physics-informed neural networks and symmetry-constrained architectures, which embed conservation laws and quantum-mechanical constraints into the learning process; and generative models — variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion-based frameworks — which can propose novel structures with pre-specified target properties. We trace the intellectual evolution of these methods, benchmark their performance on standardized datasets, and situate them within the broader context of active-learning workflows where computational prediction and experimental feedback operate in a closed loop. The evidence confirms substantial progress: GNN-based property predictors now routinely approach density functional theory accuracy at a tiny fraction of the computational expense, and conditional generative frameworks are beginning to propose experimentally synthesizable candidates that fall outside previously known chemical families. We are equally candid about what remains unresolved: the synthesis reality gap, systematic biases in training databases, poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates, and the still-limited ability to extract physically interpretable insight from deep architectures. The review closes with concrete recommendations for how the field should evolve — algorithmically, experimentally, and in terms of data infrastructure — if machine learning-guided inverse design is to deliver materials that meaningfully advance the clean energy transition.

title: Explicit Spin Regulation as an Emerging Design Paradigm in Heterogeneous Catalysis
abstract: Conspectus Catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability arise from coupled electronic, structural, interfacial, transport, and spin-related processes. Conventional catalyst design has relied largely on electronic effects, strain or stress engineering, active-site construction, and local reaction environment control. Although these strategies have enabled major advances, they do not fully capture the spin degrees of freedom associated with open-shell transition-metal centers and magnetically responsive catalysts. Spin state, spin polarization, magnetic moment, spin density, and magnetic ordering can influence adsorbate binding, transition-state stabilization, charge transfer, and reaction pathways, yet their catalytic consequences are often grouped under the broad label of magnetic enhancement without a clear mechanistic assignment. In this Account, we develop explicit spin regulation as a framework for magnetism-informed catalysis. Magnetic enhancement describes an observed response to a magnetic field, a magnetic component, or a magnetic environment. Explicit spin regulation, by contrast, requires deliberate modulation of spin-related variables at or near catalytically active sites and a mechanistic connection to catalytic function. We organize this framework around two routes. Catalyst-integrated spin levers use promoters, interfaces, or interphases to tune the active-site spin/electronic structure, whereas field-induced spin levers introduce external fields or catalyst-localized magnetic perturbations during catalysis. Although implemented differently, both routes seek to control how the active-site spin governs adsorption, transition-state energetics, charge transfer, selectivity, stability, and durability. Our studies provide representative evidence for this framework. Promoter-induced spin modulation stabilizes the N–N dissociation transition state beyond conventional electrostatic promotion, establishing the spin-promotion effect as a catalyst-integrated design principle. In electrocatalysis, external fields, embedded nanomagnets, and magnetic proximity effects provide progressively localized perturbations that can be connected to spin-sensitive active sites, key intermediates, or local magnetic ordering. These examples also show why performance enhancement alone is insufficient. A convincing assignment should connect the imposed perturbation, the active-site spin/electronic response, the affected intermediate or transition state, and the resulting catalytic consequence. Magnetic measurements, electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, element-specific X-ray spectroscopies, operando methods, kinetic analysis, and spin-polarized theory provide complementary elements of this evidence loop. Building on this mechanistic framework, we further translate the active-site spin into catalyst-design descriptors. The local metal-center spin moment can be correlated with oxygen-intermediate adsorption and activity trends, enabling descriptor-guided screening of dual-atom catalysts. Spin-related variables may also inform stability and durability through their connections to phase stability, surface reconstruction, active-site preservation, dissolution resistance, and long-term operation. Generalizing these insights requires paired, standardized, and machine-readable datasets that connect magnetic perturbations, active-site structures, spin-sensitive measurements, catalytic metrics, and durability under comparable conditions. Artificial intelligence-assisted literature mining, knowledge graph construction, high-throughput spin-polarized calculations, active learning, and magnetism-aware machine-learning interatomic potentials may help identify transferable spin descriptors and extend spin-regulated catalyst design to dynamic interfaces. The broader aim is to move magnetism-informed catalysis from phenomenological enhancement toward predictive control through deliberate regulation of the active-site spin.

title: Closing the learning loop in lithium–sulfur batteries through physics-informed and trustworthy artificial intelligence
abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries combine a high theoretical specific energy with low-cost active materials, yet their development remains constrained by coupled reaction pathways, mobile intermediates, lithium-metal instability, and a large design space that changes with loading, electrolyte inventory, temperature, format, and cycling history. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a way to connect these variables, but most published demonstrations remain isolated within small computational datasets, literature-derived tables, or single-laboratory cell series. This review develops an evidence-first, closed-loop framework for AI-enabled Li–S research that links observation, learning, decision, validation, and model updating. It critically examines data infrastructure, text and multimodal extraction, descriptor learning, catalyst and electrolyte design, physics-informed state inference, degradation prognosis, autonomous experimentation, and digital twins. The available evidence shows that machine learning (ML) can compress high-dimensional calculations, recover useful structure–property relations, and predict selected cell outcomes within bounded domains. However, ML has not yet demonstrated robust transfer across laboratories, cell formats, or practical operating conditions. The main barriers are incomplete metadata, non-independent data splits, uncertain labels, weak uncertainty calibration, and limited prospective validation. To address these gaps, the review introduces a minimum data schema, an evidence-fidelity pathway that separates proxy prediction from decision-grade evidence, task-specific benchmarking requirements, and a minimum viable digital-twin architecture for Li–S cells. The central conclusion is that AI becomes decision-grade only when its predictions are physically credible, uncertainty-aware, experimentally actionable, and iteratively validated.

title: Machine Learning‐Assisted Discovery of Unconventional Molybdenum Nitride Nano‐Facets as Hydrogen Evolution Electrocatalysts
abstract: ABSTRACT Transition‐metal nitrides (TMNs) are promising electrocatalysts owing to their unique electronic structures and surface properties. Yet, the formation of metastable phases during particle growth is unavoidable in the traditional synthesis of TMNs. These metastable phases cannot be holistically depicted by conventional phase diagrams. Here, we use density functional theory (DFT) calculations in conjunction with thermodynamic analysis to establish particle‐size‐dependent phase diagrams for Mo nitrides (Mo x N y ), including both metastable and thermodynamically stable phases. To accelerate the identification of energetically favourable high‐Miller‐index facets of Mo nitrides, we complement our DFT approach with a machine learning (ML) model trained on computed results for low‐Miller‐index facets. Furthermore, we compute hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) free energy diagrams using DFT for both low‐ and high‐Miller‐index facets, uncovering that several previously underexplored high‐Miller‐index facets of Mo nitrides are not only stable but also catalytically active for HER. Our study elucidates the correlation between nanoparticle dimension and phase stability, predicts unconventional facets of Mo nitrides that serve as good catalysts in HER, and ultimately presents a computationally guided strategy to efficiently navigate the material discovery landscape and further discover robust and efficient catalysts for green energy conversion schemes.

title: Enhanced Oxygen Reduction of Biatom Catalysts on g-CN with Heteroatom Doped: A Theoretical Investigation by Density Functional Theory and Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Biatom catalysts (BACs) are well-known as promising candidates for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). However, the vast design space of the BACs causes a high cost for experimental and computational screening. Herein, by employing density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine-learning (ML) algorithms, we propose a data-driven high-throughput design approach for the rapid screening of ORR catalysts consisting of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal dimers (TM2) inserted in pristine and heteroatom (S, C, B, P)-doped g-CN support with excellent activity. According to the DFT calculations and ML predictions, we conclude that the BACs of Ag2/Pd2-C-I, Pt2-B-I, Pd2-P-I, and Pd2/Ag2-C-II can serve as promising candidates for ORR catalysts. The ML analysis reveals that the intrinsic properties of the metal active center play a dominant role in the catalytic activity of BACs, accounting for 71.6% of the total feature importance, while the coordination environment contributes to a lesser extent of 28.4%. Thus, based on the suitable metal active center, doping C/B/P heteroatoms on the g-CN support is an effective way to further improve the catalytic activity. A bridge from intrinsic properties to catalytic activity has been established in this work, which is conducive to unveiling the origin of the ORR activity and accelerating the screening process for high-activity ORR catalysts.

title: Charge Transfer Mediators in Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting: From Interfacial Regulation to Rational Design
abstract: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting is a promising route for solar-to-chemical energy conversion and storage, yet its efficiency remains limited by interfacial charge recombination, inefficient carrier extraction, and sluggish reaction kinetics. Charge transfer mediators have emerged as critical interfacial components bridging photoelectrodes, cocatalysts, and conductive substrates, enabling directional carrier transport, suppressed recombination, and enhanced catalytic activity. However, their roles, design principles, and mechanisms in PEC systems remain insufficiently understood. This review systematically defines charge transfer mediators in PEC water splitting, clarifies their multifunctional roles in charge transfer, charge storage, and interfacial protection, and summarizes representative material platforms, including carbon-based materials, MXenes, metal oxides, molecular materials, nonmetal nitrides, and other emerging mediators. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationship between mediator structures, interfacial configurations, electronic properties, and PEC performance. Advanced characterization techniques and theoretical approaches for elucidating charge transfer pathways and reaction mechanisms are also discussed to establish structure-property-performance correlations. Finally, key challenges and future perspectives are highlighted, positioning charge transfer mediators as an emerging paradigm for constructing efficient, stable, and practical PEC systems.

title: Assessing the Transferability of General-Purpose MachineLearning Interatomic Potentials for Heterogeneous Catalysis with HetCat26
abstract: Foundation machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise near-density functional theory (DFT) accuracy across broad areas of chemistry and materials science. However, their performance in describing systems and processes relevant to heterogeneous catalysis remains underexplored. Here, we introduce HetCat26, a collection of benchmark tests designed to assess pre-trained MLIPs across key aspects of catalytic modeling, including surface energetics, metal-metal oxide interactions, adsorption, and catalytic reaction networks. Evaluating fifteen foundation models, we find that performance on existing general materials benchmarks is only weakly predictive of performance on HetCat26; transferability to heterogeneous catalysis cannot be inferred from these general benchmarks. Across the benchmark tests, current models describe surface energetics and, perhaps surprisingly, reaction barriers well, whereas larger errors are observed for adsorption, and DFT site preferences are often not reproduced. Two models, eSEN-30M-OAM and MACE-MH-1-OMAT, nevertheless achieve high accuracy across the properties evaluated. Beyond model benchmarking, HetCat26 highlights the importance of training data consistency: PBE and PBE+U calculations should not be mixed within a training set. Overall, we identify challenges limiting the transferability of current foundation MLIPs to heterogeneous catalysis and, more broadly, to chemical reactions at interfaces, providing guidance for the development of the next generation of foundation models.

title: Accelerating green heterocyclic synthesis: Convergence of AI , automation, and sustainable chemistry
journal: Bulletin of the Korean Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Heterocyclic compounds are among the most prevalent scaffolds in bioactive molecules, with approximately 82% of small‐molecule drugs approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) during 2013–2023 containing nitrogen heterocycles. Their synthesis, however, often relies on toxic solvents, stoichiometric reagents, and energy‐intensive conditions that generate substantial waste. Green chemistry strategies, including solvent‐free protocols, alternative reaction media, catalytic methods, and energy‐efficient activation, have reduced the environmental footprint of heterocyclic synthesis. However, optimal conditions are still commonly identified through trial‐and‐error experimentation. This review examines how the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and laboratory automation is addressing this bottleneck. We first survey established green synthesis strategies and their limitations. We then examine machine learning approaches for predictive reaction design and three major automation platforms—high‐throughput experimentation, continuous flow chemistry, and self‐driving laboratories—that translate these predictions into experimental practice. A central premise of this review is that incorporating quantitative green metrics, such as E‐factor and process mass intensity, as explicit objectives in AI‐driven optimization can make sustainability a prospective design criterion. Demonstrations now include heterocycle‐related pharmaceutical process development, although comparable validation across complete routes remains limited. We discuss the data infrastructure, scalability, and regulatory challenges that must be addressed to extend these results toward integrated autonomous green synthesis.

title: Pathways for the integration of bioenergetic and food production: An artificial intelligence-assisted review
abstract: ABSTRACT The application of agricultural biomass as a renewable energy source is garnering global attention, particularly for its contribution to the circular economy. However, the production pathways needed to harmonize agricultural production for alimentation and/or as a bioenergy resource remain unclear. Despite growing literature on renewable energy, a research gap persists in the integration of bioenergy into the food security framework. This research aims to identify the conditions under which bioenergy can be produced without jeopardizing food production. A methodology was developed that combined bibliometric clustering with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), providing a systematic framework for sustainable agricultural biomass and bioenergy co-production. To determine potential pathways for integrated agricultural-bioenergy production, a bibliographic analysis was conducted using the Web of Science (WoS) database and VOSviewer software. A GenAI tool and diagramming software were then used to address the question: Is it possible to produce bioenergy without affecting food production? Two groups of keywords with the highest occurrence and citations, were obtained by data mining and clustering analysis. A total of 10 pathways were identified, supported by AI, able to balance bioenergy and food production. All pathways use agricultural crop residue, food waste, manure, algae, sludge, and torrefied biomass as energy sources. This study corroborates the use of GenAI to identify bioenergetic-food integration pathways and presents a novel methodology for identifying and integrating them into the current food security framework.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Design of Cu-Based Single-Atom Alloy Nanoclusters for Selective CO2 Electroreduction
abstract: Metal nanoclusters are highly promising for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) due to their abundant low-coordination sites and size-dependent electronic properties. Alloying these clusters with isolated transition metal atoms to form Cu-based single-atom alloys (Cu-SAAs) provides a powerful strategy to finely tune their local structures and electronic properties. Because the dopant element identifies and its specific surface site strongly dictate *CO adsorption and subsequent eCO2RR pathways, systematically mapping this combinatorial space is critical. To clarify these effects, we synergistically couple high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML) to evaluate *CO adsorption across 1,944 small Cu-SAAs nanocluster candidates. Using reliable DFT-derived adsorption data, we developed an iterative Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model capable of rapidly predicting binding energies by identifying the governing structural and electronic descriptors. Analysis of these large-scale predictions highlights how specific combinations of dopant elements and geometrical sites modulate *CO adsorption strength, directly influencing catalytic trajectories. This work establishes an interpretable, data-driven framework for the rational design of Cu-SAAs nanoclusters tailored for targeted eCO2RR products.

title: Toward Mild Conditions for N2 Activation: Progress and Challenges from Nitrogenase to Biomimetic Artificial Catalysts
abstract: Abstract Nitrogen (N2), as the most abundant gas in the atmosphere, poses a long-standing challenge in chemistry and biochemistry due to its high bond energy (≈941 kJ·mol–1) and thus low reactivity under mild conditions. In nature, nitrogenase can reduce N2 to ammonia at ambient temperature and pressure, while industry relies on the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process for ammonia synthesis. This paper systematically reviews the mechanisms and catalytic progress in biological nitrogen fixation and industrial ammonia synthesis, with a focus on the structure and catalytic mechanism of nitrogenase, as well as the catalytic mechanisms and green pathways for industrial ammonia production. It further summarizes the design strategies and recent advances in artificial nitrogen fixation catalysts inspired by nitrogenase. For example, a biomimetic iron–molybdenum dual-atom catalyst on carbonized delignified wood (FeMo-CDW) recently achieved an NH3 production rate of 336.03 μg·h–1·cm–2 under acidic conditions, while an Fe single-atom catalyst supported on monolayer MoS2 delivered an NH3 production rate of 97.5 ± 6 μg·h–1·cm–2, underscoring the practical promise of nitrogenase-inspired systems. By reviewing molecular catalysts, metal sulfides/carbides, single-atom catalysts, and related directions, this review paper outlines future development pathways for efficient nitrogen fixation catalytic systems under mild conditions, offering theoretical insights and design principles for breakthroughs in green ammonia synthesis technologies.

title: Structure–Activity Relationships in Phloroglucinol‐Bridged Binuclear Versus Mononuclear Iron/Cobalt Phthalocyanine Electrocatalysts for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction: A Combined Experimental and Computational Investigation
abstract: ABSTRACT Iron and cobalt phthalocyanines (FePc and CoPc) rank among the most promising non‐precious metal electrocatalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), yet a systematic structure–activity comparison combining experimental and computational approaches remains lacking. This study examines how peripheral nitro substitution combined with a phloroglucinol bridging ligand modulates ORR activity in FeTNPc and CoTNPc in 0.1 M KOH. Rotating disk electrode (RDE) measurements showed that heteronuclear Fe–Co bridge coordination shifted the ORR pathway of FePc toward the ideal 4‐electron process ( n = 3.79, versus a more mixed‐pathway response for the monomers, particularly CoTNPc), while anodically shifting the onset potential by up to 40 mV relative to monomeric FeTNPc and CoTNPc. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and UV–Vis spectroscopy corroborated the predicted redistribution of electron density at the metal centers. Critically, density functional theory (DFT) calculations of O 2 adsorption free energy correlated quadratically with experimental half‐wave potentials ( R 2 = 0.997), and the Fe dz 2 orbital energy emerged as a reliable electronic descriptor of activity, with nitro‐substituted bimetallic FeCoPc exhibiting a narrow HOMO–LUMO gap (∼1.05 eV). These findings establish an orbital‐energy‐guided design rule for tailoring phthalocyanine electrocatalysts, offering a route to reduce PEMFC reliance on platinum‐group metals.

title: From electronic descriptors to durable design: a multi-scale review of catalysts for LOHC dehydrogenation
abstract: Liquid organic hydrogen carriers offer a dense platform for hydrogen storage, yet their deployment is hindered by catalyst deactivation and energy demand. This review provides a mechanism-focused synthesis connecting atomic-scale electronic descriptors to catalyst formulation and reactor performance. We revisit Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi relationships, volcano trends, and electronic modulation as conditional tools for interpreting C-H activation. These principles rationalize alloying strategies: Pt-Sn illustrates activity–stability trade-offs; Pt-Pd tailors adsorption energetics; supported Pt-Ir illustrates preparation-dependent dispersion. We also examine metal–support interactions on oxides, mesoporous silicas, and carbon matrices that enable confinement and spillover. Integrating these insights, we outline a multi-scale design perspective linking electronic descriptors to surface kinetics, framing durability as a central criterion. The review concludes with opportunities in data-driven discovery, operando deactivation mapping, and process optimization, emphasizing green-chemistry priorities of efficiency, selectivity, reduced critical-metal use, and long-term stability.

title: A green solvent screening tool for emerging materials via uncertainty aware, transformer enhanced transfer learning
abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of solubility remains a central challenge across materials science and sustainable chemistry. In particular, due to emerging technologies like organic and hybrid photovoltaics, batteries, and catalysis, solvent usage is expected to increase significantly within the coming years. Therefore, substituting solvents with greener alternatives is vital. This is where machine learning can make a substantial impact. However, the limited data on critical parameters of solubility significantly constraints machine learning efficacy. In this work, we transfer a pre-trained foundational model on QM9 targets to our application with minimal data requirements. Additionally, the pipeline integrates uncertainty quantification, allowing the user to gauge the confidence of the predictions. As baseline, we succeed in predicting the Hansen solubility parameters and Dielectric Constant for which extensive databases exist. Importantly, we achieve high model performance on additional targets, such as Gutmann Donor and Acceptor numbers, where the available data is extremely limited. Overall, we augment data on solubility descriptors by up to two orders of magnitude with high-quality predictions. For effective dissemination, we deploy an easy-to-use, easily integratable with high throughput labs, customizable tool for ranking and screening possible solvent substitutes. Finally, we both rediscovered known green solvent alternatives and proposed new candidates, proving its relevance for finding eco-friendly solvents.

title: Fine-tuning large language models to generate single-atom catalyst synthesis procedures
abstract: Heterogeneous catalyst design is primarily expert-driven and difficult to keep track amidst rapidly growing literature, motivating the use of large language models (LLMs) to learn from existing knowledge. While generalist LLMs show some capability in generating synthesis procedures, they struggle on encountering complex catalytic systems like single-atom catalysts (SAC). Here, we investigate fine-tuning of LLMs to improve the generation of SAC synthesis procedures with chemical relevance. We curate a dataset of 2,964 SAC publications and train the Granite-based LLM to recommend protocols based on user-defined prompts including metal-support combinations, synthesis method, and target reactions. We demonstrate the model's practicality through a user interface allowing researchers to query procedures tailored to their design conditions. Human-in-the-loop validation of 150 model-generated SAC protocols confirmed coherent, context-aware procedures with synthesis sequence steps that align with experimental logic, along with limitations. We underscore LLM-generated protocols must be critically reviewed and used as assistive tools, and highlight fine-tuned LLMs for AI-assisted synthesis planning driving innovation in catalysis research.

title: Physics-Guided Design of Ammonia Decomposition Catalysts with Interpretable Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Rational catalyst design for ammonia decomposition requires navigating coupled structural and electronic effects that govern reaction energetics across a large configurational space. Here, we integrate density functional theory (DFT), microkinetic modeling (MKM), and interpretable machine learning to establish a physics-guided screening framework. For the most active stepped Ru(10–13) surface, MKM identifies NH* dissociation as the rate-limiting step and defines an NH* binding-energy window of -4.47 to -3.84 eV that sustains near-maximal turnover frequency across 673–750 K and applied fields of 0 and − 0.4 V/Å. A DFT database comprising 1,132 Ru and 270 Co configurations spanning surface structure, adatom coverage, and electronic state was used to train a gradient-boosted model, achieving a Ru test mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.082 eV. Although direct Ru-to-Co transfer yields a 0.397 eV error, incorporating only 45 Co configurations reduces the Co test MAE to 0.120 eV. SHAP analysis identifies charge, local site coordination, and surface energy as the dominant factors governing NH* binding. Guided by these relationships, screening ~ 33,000 physically constructed candidates enriches the population within the kinetic target, while constrained-DFT validation supports the model’s ability to identify promising configurations.

title: Ioc-Mldroid: a Hybrid Approach for Detection of Android Based Malicious Applications Using Indicators of Compromise (Iocs) and Machine Learning
abstract: Android operating system has taken over the mobile ecosystem across the world and thus is a prime target of more advanced malware that uses its ability to obfuscate, dynamically load code, encrypted communications and even environment aware evasion behaviors. These properties severely circumscribe the ability of conventional signature-based detection systems, and are problematic to either all-static or all-dynamic analysis. Although machine learning-based detection methods have promise, most current solutions are black-box systems with no forensic transparency [5][6] , and are not as applicable in security operations and digital investigations. This paper presents an android malware detection system being a hybrid between the static-dynamic framework and powered by Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) and machine learning. The framework uses a constrained dual-VM setup consisting of an analysis host based on Ubuntu and an instrumented android emulator. Standard analysis tools are used to extract the static IoCs, which consist of permissions, manifest components, use of sensitive APIs, cryptographic artifacts, certificate metadata, and embedded network indicators. Controlled application execution can be used to obtain dynamic IoCs by monitoring and instrumenting runtime behaviors related to behavioural indicators like network communication, filesystem activity and sensitive API invocation. A framework IoC correlation and normalization engine is used to combine heterogeneous non-uniform indicators which are static and dynamic, into structured feature vectors. A random Forest model that has been chosen due to its strong ability to predict high-dimensional data, as well as the ability to have an interpretable component, are used to classify these vectors. In addition to binary classification, the framework produces a structured forensic intelligence report, which records the IoCs behind each detection decision, which in turn facilitates evidence-based and explainable malware detection. The suggested framework puts the emphasis on the detectability, interpretability and forensic relevance. It improves resilience to evasion by obfuscation, but does not increase decision-making transparency through the correlation of fixating and moving IoCs. The work provides an expandable and explainable android malware detection architecture that can be used in academic research, enterprise security operations, and advanced digital forensic investigation, and which may be extended in the future to the scale of validation and on-device detection.

title: ReactionAtlas: Ab origine exploration of chemical reaction networks with machine learning
abstract: Mapping a chemical reaction network, the graph of minima and transition states (TS) and the elementary reactions connecting them, is the natural language of chemistry, from catalysis to combustion to the origin of life. Constructing such a reaction network for a given chemistry has been impractical: it requires finding and characterizing tens of thousands of TS, a task for which traditional methods such as density functional theory (DFT) are typically prohibitively slow and require reactant and product as input. We introduce ReactionAtlas, which builds a reaction network $\textit{ab origine}$ from a handful of seed molecules and without hand-crafted rules. Specifically, our machine-learned generative model proposes reactions from kinetically sampled candidate compounds and a DFT-trained machine learned force field (MLFF) filters them to valid TS, the resulting products of which enter the search as new seeds. Starting from eight pre-biotic seeds (CH$_2$O, H$_2$O, OH$^-$, H$_3$O$^+$, CO$_2$, H$_2$CO$_3$, HCO$_3^-$, H), ReactionAtlas discovers $\sim$47,000 reactions among $\sim$12,000 compounds. The MLFF TSs match the PBE0 references within 0.5 Å RMSD in 85% of the cases and can be easily brought to the PBE0 level. Thus, ReactionAtlas maps small carbohydrate chemistry up to C$_4$H$_8$O$_4$ at unprecedented scale and accuracy, including charge and stereo information. It enables novel insights into many well-studied reaction paths, including the formose cycle, which we highlight for its centrality to the chemical origins of life. Notably, our framework also allows establishing alternative reaction pathways for formose chemistry.

title: Feature Selection in Multivariate Linear Regression Models for Data-Efficient Reaction Optimization
abstract: Abstract We introduce NaviCat ReaFS (reaction feature selection), a framework for testing and supporting multivariate linear regression models for reaction optimization in small, heterogeneous datasets, where overfitting risk is high and additional experiments are costly. ReaFS combines systematic benchmarking of feature selection methods with targeted diagnostics spanning data, feature-subsets, and predictions. We also introduce a composite score that captures complementary aspects of extrapolative performance, namely, candidate recovery, predictive accuracy, and ranking quality, enabling direct comparison of models and feature selection strategies across homogeneous catalysis datasets. ReaFS further integrates cross-validation schemes, data and feature diagnostics, and robustness checks for prospective model assessment. Together, these components provide a practical route to more informed decision-making in low-data reaction optimization.

title: Selenium‐Induced Interplay Between Processing, Phase Stability, and Hydrogen Evolution in Multicomponent Pentlandites
abstract: Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance of selenium‐rich multicomponent pentlandites was investigated using the Co 9 −x −y Fe x Ni y S 4 Se 4 series prepared as powders, as‐cast ingots, and induction‐hot‐pressed pellets. Structural, electrochemical, spectroscopic, and density functional theory analyses were combined to establish composition‐structure–activity relationships. Selenium extends the single‐phase range after synthesis but promotes partial phase separation during processing, particularly in Fe‐rich compositions. Although the effect of cationic composition on HER performance is comparatively weak within the investigated Se‐rich series, making the catalytic response increasingly dependent on electrode architecture and phase stability, the best HER performance across all material forms is consistently near the equimolar composition but shifted toward the Fe─Co‐rich region, whereas Ni‐rich compositions remain less active. Fe‐rich pellets show the highest activity ( η 20 = 200 mV) together with pronounced surface reconstruction and preferential iron dissolution, while compositions closer to the equimolar region exhibit higher overpotentials ( η 20 = 251–256 mV) with greater stability, revealing a composition‐dependent balance between activity and structural stability. Calculations indicate that selenium shifts the d‐band center toward the Fermi level and strengthens hydrogen adsorption, contributing to sluggish HER kinetics. Overall, selenium suppresses the beneficial activation characteristic of sulfur‐rich systems and fundamentally changes the factors governing HER performance, making it increasingly dependent on phase stability and electrode architecture.

title: DASyR-LLM: Domain-Aware Symbolic Regression with LLMs for Kinetic Model Discovery
abstract: Kinetic model discovery is a central challenge in chemical engineering, as accurate rate expressions are essential for understanding and controlling chemical and biological processes. Symbolic regression (SR) has emerged as a powerful data-driven approach for identifying interpretable kinetic models, but usually operates without domain knowledge, often exploring physicochemically implausible models. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for injecting domain expertise into this search. Here, we introduce an LLM-guided SR framework, embedding an LLM module within an iterative SR algorithm for automated kinetic model discovery. The LLM performs two roles at each iteration: (1) a qualitative physicochemical critique of the best SR candidates, and (2) the proposal of new candidate rate expressions guided by the SR-generated models and embedded chemical knowledge. Our framework is evaluated on four in silico case studies of increasing complexity, spanning heterogeneous catalysis and bioprocess systems. Results show the LLM-guided framework reduces iterations to identify the ground-truth model by $41.7-79.3\%$ versus a state-of-the-art SR framework, with the LLM directly proposing the correct model structure in over half of the guided runs. In practical settings, where each iteration typically requires a new wet-lab experiment, this translates into a substantial reduction in experimental effort. Predictive performance on an independent validation set is equivalent between both approaches, with $R^2>0.98$ in all case studies. Ablation studies indicate that both the SR component and the LLM scale contribute to this performance, with a reduced-size LLM largely retaining discovery efficiency. These findings demonstrate that LLMs can effectively inject domain knowledge into scientific model discovery, paving the way toward fully automated, domain-aware kinetic modelling pipelines.

title: Automated Exploration of Complex Reaction Networks Accelerated by a Data-Efficient Machine Learning Potential
abstract: Accurate and transferable machine learning potentials (MLPs) for reactive systems require datasets capturing elusive non-equilibrium geometries. Here we present an integrated molecular dynamics/coordinate driving-active learning (MD/CD-AL) framework that efficiently samples diverse reactive configurations to construct MDCD20, a curated dataset of ~1.4 million H/C/N/O structures with radical species covered. Trained on MDCD20, the resulting MDCD-NN MLP achieves quantum-mechanical accuracy in reaction pathway predictions, matching or surpassing existing MLPs trained on much larger datasets. Tests across 181 widespread types of elementary reactions confirm excellent transferability. Leveraging MD/CD-driven automatic searching, MDCD-NN serves as an effective tool for constructing reaction networks with a 104-fold speedup relative to its reference density functional theory calculations. Its capacity could be demonstrated by rationalizing and extending experimentally established mechanisms in three real-world reactions, tackling complex scenarios such as multiple reaction centers, large conformational spaces, enantioselectivity. MDCD-NN also supports nanosecond-scale dynamics to map reactive free-energy landscapes. This work establishes a data-efficient paradigm for building reactive MLPs, enabling high-throughput mechanistic exploration in chemically complex reactions.

title: Expanding frontiers of complex reaction network exploration through a general reactive machine learning potential
abstract: Abstract Developing general machine learning potentials (MLPs) for complex reactive systems remains a fundamental challenge, due to insufficient sampling of critical transition states (TSs) and non-equilibrium structures in training datasets. Here, we introduce an MD/CD-AL framework integrating molecular dynamics/coordinate driving (MD/CD) method with active learning to generate the MDCD20 dataset that encompasses diverse reactive configurations with up to 20 heavy atoms. With this dataset, we develop a general reactive MLP with quantum mechanics (QM) accuracy, MDCD-NN, for H-/C-/N-/O-containing gas-phase reactions. Leveraging MD/CD searching, MDCD-NN enables automated and efficient construction of complex reaction networks with 104-fold acceleration compared to the reference QM method, as demonstrated in three real-world reaction systems featuring intricate regio-/stereo-selectivities. In each case, our approach successfully identifies thousands of intermediates and TSs, constructing multistep networks that rationalize experimental observations and extend established mechanisms. Furthermore, MDCD-NN enables nanosecond-scale dynamics simulations for calculating reactive free energy surface, bridging quantum-level accuracy with scalable simulations. Our framework provides a paradigm for developing general reactive MLPs, enabling high-throughput mechanistic insights for complex chemical systems.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven platform for catalytic reactor discovery and optimization applied to carbon dioxide valorization
abstract: Digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and additive manufacturing advancements, have revolutionized all areas of chemistry and chemical engineering. In the field of reactor engineering, the development of novel geometries has enabled improved performance. However, until now the design has been largely relying on human design. This study introduces Reac-Discovery, a digital platform that integrates the generation, fabrication, and optimization of catalytic reactors based on periodic open-cell structures (POCs). It integrates the parametric design and analysis of advanced structures from mathematic models (Reac-Gen), the high-resolution 3D printing and functionalization of catalytic reactors (Reac-Fab) with an algorithm that validates the printability of reactor designs and a self-driving laboratory platform (Reac-Eval) capable of parallel multi-reactor evaluations featuring real-time NMR monitoring and machine learning (ML) simultaneous optimization of process parameters and topologic descriptors. Reac-Discovery can iteratively, dynamically, and rapidly refine reactor designs and reaction conditions, enabling the discovery of optimal geometries for industrially relevant processes. The heterogeneously catalyzed CO₂ cycloaddition at low pressure was chosen as a benchmark reaction. Reac-Discovery offered an improvement of ca. one order of magnitude over the state of the art. By seamlessly integrating digital design and machine learning, Reac-Discovery establishes a transformative framework for advancing complex chemical systems.
